messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 53

He is seventy-two now, a South Eastern Asian man with a gentle, deliberate way of speaking that makes people lean in. He has been married for nearly five decades, and for most of his adult life he has been the person others turn to in crisis. He works in refugee aid, helping newly arrived families fill out forms, find housing, and navigate offices that seem designed to exhaust them. He says he chose the work because he knows what it means to live with fear and uncertainty, though for many years he told that part of his life only in fragments.

The event he returns to began more than thirty years ago, when he was working at a provincial administrative office in his home country. It was an ordinary morning by his telling: papers stacked on a desk, a ceiling fan stirring hot air, the sound of motorcycles and vendors outside. Then armed men entered the building. He remembers the sharp crack of gunfire before he fully understands what is happening. He sees one colleague fall beside a cabinet, another trying to crawl under a table. He throws himself to the floor and presses his face against the dusty tile, convinced each second will be his last. He can smell smoke and something metallic he later knows is blood. At one point a boot stops near his head, and he holds his breath so completely that his chest burns. The men shout political slogans. He hears screaming in another room, then an explosion that shakes plaster from the ceiling.

He survives by remaining still among overturned chairs and shattered glass until the attackers leave. When he finally rises, his legs barely hold him. He helps carry the wounded outside, but one of the men he lifts is already dead. For weeks afterward, he tells himself survival means he must not waste time on fear. His country is unstable, and he and his wife soon flee. In the chaos of displacement, there is always another practical problem to solve. He believes, or tries to believe, that staying useful will keep memory contained.

In the first years after resettlement, he works constantly. He learns a new language, takes whatever jobs are available, and later finds his way into refugee services. He is admired for his calm under pressure. Families notice that he does not flinch at bureaucratic confusion or raised voices. He can sit with people as they recount terrible losses, and he rarely interrupts. But at home his wife sees another side. He startles violently when a car backfires. If someone approaches him from behind, he spins around with his fists half raised before he seems to recognize where he is. At night he sleeps lightly, waking drenched in sweat after dreams in which he is back on the floor of that office, unable to move while footsteps come closer. Sometimes he shouts in his sleep in a language he barely uses during the day.

Over the years he becomes skilled at arranging his world to avoid reminders. He does not enter government buildings without first locating the exits. He chooses chairs facing the door in restaurants, community meetings, even at family gatherings. National news about bombings or political violence leaves him agitated for hours, though he insists he is only “concerned.” His wife has learned not to touch him unexpectedly when he is concentrating, especially if he is reading reports from conflict zones. On those days his jaw tightens, and he becomes distant, answering in short phrases. Their children, now grown, tease him gently about checking locks two and three times before bed, but they also know there are subjects that close him off completely.

His work both sustains and strains him. He feels most alive when he is helping a frightened family settle into an apartment or accompanying an elder to a medical appointment. Yet certain details undo him: the smell of concrete dust from a damaged building, a client describing masked men with guns, a child dropping to the floor during a loud noise. He says there are moments in the office when the present “slides away.” He is looking at a client across the desk, and suddenly he is no longer an old man in a safe country but a younger man listening for boots on tile. During these episodes his heart races and his shirt clings to his back. He forces himself to keep nodding, to keep writing, while inside he is fighting the urge to run.

Lately the symptoms feel harder to contain. Retirement age has come and gone, but he continues working part-time, saying he fears what will happen if he has too much time to think. Since a terrorist attack at a transit station in the city two years ago, his world has narrowed further. He avoids trains, crowded lobbies, and public ceremonies. He scans strangers’ hands and bags without meaning to. He is tired all the time, yet dreads going to sleep. His wife says he is physically present but often far away. He agrees. He tells her he has spent decades building a life devoted to helping people escape danger, but some part of him still lives on that office floor, listening, waiting, certain the next shot is meant for him.
